tagline: A river canyon, hairpin grades and an Olympic mountain pass
intro: US 50 climbs the South Fork American River canyon, crosses the Sierra Nevada at Echo Summit and descends into the Lake Tahoe Basin. Much of that mountain crossing is two lanes, with hairpin turns east of Strawberry. The highway east of SR 49 belongs to the State Scenic Highway System except within South Lake Tahoe city limits.

In 1852, John Calhoun Johnson of Placerville cleared a shorter, lower trail east from town. His cutoff generally followed the present US 50 corridor, but crossed the crest at Johnson Pass. El Dorado County bought the privately improved sections in 1886 and ended toll collection. California authorized its first state road along this corridor in 1895; US 50 followed in 1926. State maintenance brought granite milestones marking distance from Placerville, followed in 1910 by summer watering to suppress dust on the dirt road. Later paving projects bypassed sections of the old alignment.

Driving east from Placerville, the last freeway section runs from near Camino to the east end of Pollock Pines. The road enters the canyon near Riverton, then rises past Kyburz and Strawberry to Echo Summit. Beyond the pass, it descends a steep hillside into the Tahoe Basin and turns north toward South Lake Tahoe.

moments.title: Kyburz
moments.text: Kyburz takes its name from a postmaster’s family, but its earlier names belonged to the road: Slippery Ford, then Slipperyford. Albert Kyburz made the change in 1911 to honor his father Samuel, an early California pioneer associated with John Sutter. Settlement began a mile west at Webster’s Sugar Loaf House, a Pony Express remount station, in 1860. By 1916 the locale lay on the Lincoln Highway’s Sierra Nevada Southern Route. The community sits beside US 50 and the South Fork, surrounded by the Eldorado National Forest. The post office had opened under the Slippery Ford name in 1861.

moments.title: Strawberry
moments.text: Strawberry’s place on the South Fork joined resort travel to the mail route: the town became a popular resort in the 1850s and a Pony Express station. It later lay on the Lincoln Highway’s Sierra Nevada Southern Route. The community is also home to the Lovers Leap climbing area. Just south of Route 50, the granite cliffs extend for more than a third of a mile, rising between 250 and 600 feet. The historic Pony Express trail runs directly beneath the rock face. Climbers use the granite dikes as holds on many routes.
moments.notice: Lover’s Leap forms a steep granite cliff band south of Route 50.

moments.title: Echo Summit
moments.text: A ski-area parking lot became an Olympic proving ground at Echo Summit in 1968. The men’s track and field trials took place here a month before the Mexico City Olympics. The site first opened as a training camp for high-altitude acclimation, at an elevation similar to the Olympic stadium’s. Hundreds of Ponderosa pines remained inside the track, and boulders surrounded the high jump pit. The removable track went to South Tahoe Middle School the next summer; a roadside historical landmark sign followed in 2014. Four world records were set at the trials.
moments.notice: A historical landmark sign beside Highway 50 marks the Olympic trials site.
